# Judith Chapter 12 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Codex Vaticanus, Judith 12

---

**1** He commanded that she be brought to where his silver vessels were set out, and he ordered that she be served from his own food and his own wine.

**2** But Judith said, "I cannot eat of these things, lest it be an offense to me; what I have brought with me will be sufficient."

**3** Holofernes said to her, "But if what you have brought runs out, where can we get more of the same kind to provide for you? For none of your people are with us."

**4** Judith said to him, "As your soul lives, my lord, your servant will not exhaust what she has with her before the LORD accomplishes by my hand what he has purposed."

**5** Then the servants of Holofernes led her to the tent, and she slept until midnight. Before the morning watch she rose and sent word to Holofernes, saying,

**6** "Let my lord give orders that your servant be allowed to go out for prayer."

**7** Holofernes commanded his guard not to hinder her. She remained in the camp three days and went out each night to the valley of Bethulia, where she bathed herself at the spring in the camp.

**8** And when she came up from the water, she prayed to the LORD God of Israel to direct her way for the uplifting of the sons of his people.

**9** She returned clean and stayed in the tent until she took her food toward evening.

**10** On the fourth day Holofernes gave a banquet for his personal servants alone and did not invite any of his officers.

**11** He said to Bagoas the eunuch, who had charge of all his affairs, "Go now and persuade this Hebrew woman who is in your care to come and join us, to eat and drink in our company.

**12** For it is a disgrace to us if we let such a woman go without lying with her. If we do not win her over, she will laugh at us."

**13** Bagoas withdrew from Holofernes' presence and came to her and said, "Let this fair young woman not hesitate to come to my lord and be honored in his presence, to drink wine with us in good cheer, and to become today like one of the daughters of the Assyrians who serve in the house of Nebuchadnezzar."

**14** Judith said to him, "Who am I to refuse my lord? Whatever is pleasing in his sight I will do at once; and this will be my joy until the day of my death."

**15** She rose and dressed herself in her garments and all her woman's adornment. Her servant went ahead and spread before Holofernes on the floor the fleeces she had received from Bagoas for her daily use, so that she might recline upon them to eat.

**16** Judith came in and reclined, and Holofernes' heart was ravished at the sight of her. His soul was shaken with desire, and he was exceedingly eager to lie with her; for he had been seeking an opportunity to seduce her from the first day he had seen her.

**17** Holofernes said to her, "Now drink and be merry with us."

**18** Judith said, "I will gladly drink now, my lord, for today my life is exalted above all my days since I was born."

**19** Then she took what her servant had prepared and ate and drank before him.

**20** And Holofernes was greatly pleased with her and drank a great deal of wine — more than he had drunk on any single day since he was born.

---

### Council Notes

**On v. 4 (Judith's oath by Holofernes' soul):** All three agents note the irony: Judith swears by Holofernes' "soul" (psyche) that she will not run out of provisions before the LORD's purpose is accomplished. She is telling the complete truth. She will not run out — because the LORD's purpose will be accomplished tonight.

**On v. 7 (three-day routine):** The three-day pattern carries typological weight. PNEUMA notes correctly that the routine functions both as piety and as alibi — the guards become accustomed to her nightly departures, removing suspicion.

**On v. 12 (Holofernes' explicit intention):** All three agents agree that the explicitness must be retained. Sanitizing this verse would obscure the mortal danger Judith faces and the gravity of what she is about to do. The stakes are her honor and her life.

**On v. 15 (fleeces from Bagoas):** A logistical detail the author includes to establish the scene precisely. Judith is reclining in the posture of a banquet guest, in Holofernes' tent, on cushions provided by his own household manager.

**On v. 16 (Holofernes' desire):** The Greek is detailed and unambiguous. EMET's "ravished" for the heart metaphor is appropriately strong. SOPHIA retains this rendering.

**On v. 18 (Judith's toast):** This is the pivot verse of the chapter and perhaps the most ironic line in the book. "My life is exalted above all my days" — true in every sense she does not intend Holofernes to understand. The verb emegalunthē will echo in ch. 16's song of praise.

**On v. 20 (Holofernes' drinking):** The author is careful: Holofernes' incapacitation is entirely of his own making. He chose to drink to excess. Divine judgment works through human choice.
